📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:.

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

In a recent development, without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

It has been revealed that key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:.

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:.

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

According to recent reports, for FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

It has been revealed that do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate strategy. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

Sources indicate that for most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

In a recent development, yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Industry observers note that review your estate initiative every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a latest state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more key than for conventional retirees.

Recent findings suggest that estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate blueprint: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

David Rockwell Takes Us Inside the Design of Skywalker Grill

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe.
  • Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch, the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California.
  • In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project, Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe. But when David Rockwell and his team began developing Skywalker Grill, the signature restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the conversation went in a different direction.

Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch, the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, envisioned a space that felt warm, intimate, and welcoming, a deliberate contrast to the futuristic architecture of the museum designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects.

In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project, Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.

“They wanted to start the conversation around warmth and the kind of warmth of Skywalker Ranch in many facets, not only material palette but also custom furniture,” Rockwell explains.

That direction ultimately led to an interior defined by rich cherry wood, curved banquettes, custom furnishings, and carefully integrated lighting. One of its most striking features is a continuous wood shell that wraps from ceiling to walls, creating an almost cocoon-like environment. According to Rockwell, there isn’t a single right angle in the restaurant.

Sources indicate that achieving that effect was considerably more complicated than it appears. Each cherry wood panel was individually fabricated using a combination of traditional woodworking and technology-enabled techniques. Behind the seamless surfaces, the team also had to accommodate seismic requirements, mechanical systems, lighting, and acoustics.

In a recent development, when Paron asks what proved most challenging during the project, Rockwell points to the engineering behind the wood shell. “If I had to pinpoint one element, it would be developing the system to mount and support the cherry wood panels in such an organic design,” he recalls.

It has been revealed that the conversation also explores how the team approached the restaurant’s relationship with the surrounding museum. While the building’s sweeping forms and futuristic character could have encouraged a more theatrical interior, Rockwell and his clients were interested in something subtler.

Sources indicate that instead of incorporating recognizable cinematic imagery, the design borrows from filmmaking’s use of light, movement, and framing. A curved bar directs attention toward panoramic views of Los Angeles, while the lighting was carefully designed to avoid reflections in the expansive glass walls.

In a recent development, even the furniture placement was considered from an unusually cinematic perspective: Rockwell Group created renderings from every seat in the restaurant. “We’ve never had anyone ask us to look at that from that specific point of view,” Rockwell shares.

Throughout the episode, Rockwell offers a behind-the-scenes look at his collaboration with Lucas and Hobson, who were closely involved in the design process, reviewing mockups, testing furniture, and helping shape the restaurant’s many details.

Listen to the latest episode of Once Upon a Project to hear the full conversation between host AJ Paron and David Rockwell.

This season of Once Upon a Project is presented by Crypton.

Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood.
  • Industry observers note that burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s.
  • Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Industry observers note that burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Recent findings suggest that bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Recent findings suggest that “Burlwood does what a great print does,” notes Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”.

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

It has been revealed that the tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts, while colorful glass candlesticks and art books add color to the display. Photography by Ellen Renee.

For Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he says. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”.

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

According to recent reports, “The material is timeless,” Brooks notes. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”.

A honey-toned burlwood table features a richly figured top and tapered legs, standing out against the darker wood cabinetry behind it. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-new piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he claims, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

Industry observers note that A burlwood nightstand introduces warmth and a touch of traditional detail to this otherwise contemporary bedroom, adding a rich wood accent against the sculptural charcoal headboard and modern lines. Photography by Nick Sargent.

Sources indicate that maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he says.

In a recent development, while Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she indicates. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”.

According to recent reports, A close-up reveals the distinctive natural markings of a burlwood table, with brass-and-acrylic drawer pulls adding a mix of warm and modern finishes. Photography by Emily Hart.

Because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she states. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

A burlwood tray with a gold-toned rim highlights the wood’s warm coloring and varied markings, with stacked books providing a colorful backdrop. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

It has been revealed that for a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

According to recent reports, A curved burlwood console showcases the wood’s richly varied grain across its drawer fronts and rounded frame, with pale green stools and white fringe adding a touch of color and texture. Photography by Emily Hart.

Industry observers note that burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she indicates. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Industry observers note that maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.

A burlwood coffee table showcases the wood’s warm tones and naturally irregular markings, while art books and a decorative bowl give the tabletop a relaxed, collected feel. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Contemporary furniture designs also explore the interplay between burlwood, contrasting materials, and simpler silhouettes. Jonathan Adler’s Bond collection, for example, combines burl with acrylic on a dresser and metal on a dining table. Meacham points to Made Goods’ Bradley mirror, which lets the mappa burl frame take center stage. Fenimore recommends looking at brands like Modway and TOV Furniture, particularly for smaller items such as chairs, ottomans, and drink tables with burl accents.

Sources indicate that the rich, swirling grain of the half-moon burlwood console complements the delicate branches and floral motifs in the botanical artwork above. Photography by Emily Hart.

Sources indicate that for anyone hesitant to introduce such a distinctive material, the designers recommend beginning with one piece, such as a side table, mirror, or tray. Brooks suggests starting with something that serves an existing need, even if it’s as small as a drink table next to a chair. Maestri puts it simply: “Pick one piece and let it be the star. Keep what’s around it simpler so the grain can stand out.”.

Sources indicate that fenimore encourages mixing burlwood with other wood tones rather than trying to match everything. She also sees the material as a way to ground a room that already has plenty of color and pattern. Meacham recommends giving the grain some breathing room through intentional styling and a variety of finishes. “That doesn’t mean everything else needs to be neutral—I love burl with color—but you want your eye to have somewhere to rest.”.

Sources indicate that burlwood’s latest resurgence doesn’t require a revival of any particular decorating style. The same material that characterized Art Deco cabinetry and 1970s furniture feels equally at home alongside contemporary silhouettes, unexpected colors, and contrasting finishes. Its history is part of its appeal, but it needn’t dictate how we use it.

Recent findings suggest that there’s something particularly satisfying about finding a great gift at a reasonable price point. And when it comes to design, a smaller price tag doesn’t have to mean settling for something ordinary. Some of the most memorable objects are also the simplest: a cleverly designed kitchen tool, a colorful accessory, or an everyday essential with an unexpected twist.

For this year’s selection, we’re looking for gifts that bring a little more personality to the everyday. Think playful forms, interesting materials, useful details, and objects that reflect the creativity of the people who designed them. Whether you’re shopping for a friend, a coworker, or someone who’s notoriously difficult to buy for, these gifts under $50 offer plenty of reasons to think beyond the usual suspects.

Photography courtesy of Shelton Metal.

Inspired by treasures found along the seafloor, these miniature spoons bring an unexpected sculptural element to everyday rituals. Jewelry and homeware designer Colby Shelton Byrd hand-carves the shell-inspired forms, which are cast in solid brass and designed to develop a natural patina over time. The two-piece set is equally suited to stirring espresso or serving sugar, salt, and other small accompaniments.

The Shell Espresso Spoon Set is available at bloomingdales.com for $42.

Photography courtesy of Original Duckhead.

Industry observers note that rainy days get a little more colorful with Original Duckhead’s Matisse-inspired umbrella. Its graphic canopy is made from recycled plastic bottles, while a carved wooden duck-head handle adds an unexpected touch of whimsy. Designed with a wind-resistant frame and automatic opening mechanism, the compact umbrella combines everyday practicality with enough personality to make even a gloomy forecast feel more interesting.

The Matisse Duck Umbrella is available at originalduckhead.com for $45.

Who claims a toolbox has to live in the garage? Made in Japan from durable steel, Niwaki’s Y-Type Tool Box brings a little personality to everyday organization with its distinctive pitched lid, rounded edges, and compact industrial design. Available in yellow or gray, it’s just as useful for storing art supplies, sewing essentials, or desk accessories as it is for actual tools. At approximately 14 inches long, it’s a practical little storage solution that looks good enough to leave out.

The Niwaki Y-Type Tool Box is available at goodeeworld.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Present & Correct.

A planner that’s as thoughtfully designed on the outside as it is on the inside. The 1Y 52W 365D Planner pairs a bold, striped cover with textured paper and foil lettering for a graphic take on everyday organization. Inside, 208 pages provide space to map out the year, while the undated format means there’s no pressure to start on January 1. A ribbon bookmark adds a practical finishing touch.

The 1Y 52W 365D Planner is available at presentandcorrect.com for $47.

Tech Report: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • It has been revealed that mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Sources indicate that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

It has been revealed that mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Sources indicate that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

The museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Industry observers note that objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

In a recent development, the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.

This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

It has been revealed that the earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

According to recent reports, the other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a upcoming display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Cara de Vaca Brand Identity Is a Masterclass in Branding

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (476 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.
  • In a recent development, cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks.
  • The logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

In a recent development, cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

The logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen shows the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

Industry observers note that the lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

It has been revealed that the posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

The system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

It has been revealed that inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

It has been revealed that the website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.

See more from Anagrama on their website.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • Recent findings suggest that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

Recent findings suggest that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the New York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

In a recent development, sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

Sources indicate that in response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

In a recent development, urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

Comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the Latest York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Industry observers note that following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a fresh owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

Recent findings suggest that the terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

According to recent reports, martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

Recent findings suggest that martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

In a recent development, his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Sources indicate that AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

According to recent reports, one of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Recent findings suggest that because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

In a recent development, the token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

According to recent reports, an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

It has been revealed that ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

Industry observers note that the more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

Kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am at the moment VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

We created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

In a recent development, next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

After our pilot study with this newly introduced group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

According to recent reports, I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

We ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

According to recent reports, all participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

Recent findings suggest that I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as challenges. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Industry observers note that issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an concern is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Recent findings suggest that let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

According to recent reports, this site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall issues and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

Recent findings suggest that on this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more issues and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most challenges.

Sources indicate that here, cognitive participants found 6 more challenges and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

It has been revealed that on this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more complications and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

It has been revealed that something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more complications on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

The other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more issues with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped complications by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Sources indicate that let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability problems, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared concerns and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more problems related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

According to recent reports, in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load challenges consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

Recent findings suggest that these are improvements that would give all consumers more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but important concerns with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

Anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout rapidly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of people, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

These issues likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study revealed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

You create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability issues start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some owners.

The percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

People with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability problems that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology customers is still very vital, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Industry observers note that cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

According to recent reports, in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more complications and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

Cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

According to recent reports, this study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

In a recent development, different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the issue and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

According to recent reports, we have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

Recent findings suggest that the current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

What truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

Yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

Sources indicate that when this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

Sources indicate that if you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

In the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

It has been revealed that meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a manufacturer called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

Industry observers note that while these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

They say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

Outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

In a recent development, however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

On the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

Industry observers note that as humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

In a recent development, the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very promptly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

In a recent development, there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

According to recent reports, the dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

If history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

According to recent reports, the upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too big to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

Industry observers note that in the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

This shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

Recent findings suggest that as the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

  • Sources indicate that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • According to recent reports, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

Sources indicate that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report claims.

According to recent reports, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report states. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also indicated that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

The importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among fresh collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

According to recent reports, but can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

The report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data indicated that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

#137635. Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

📅 2026-06-16 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3441 w)
