Alphamarkâs web design for Studio Plato pairs a locked split-screen diptych with rippled glass transitions and stark white project pages.

According to recent reports, studio Platoâs homepage doesnât scroll at all. Designed and developed by Alphamark for the interior architecture practice, the landing screen locks into a full-viewport 50/50 diptych where two views of the same room share one frame. On the opening slide for Tiny Apartment in New York City, a dark walnut kitchen and sheer linen curtain anchor the left column while a wide living area sits on the right. Navigation floats straight across the photography in white: a bold uppercase PLATO wordmark beside a two-line tagline on the left, four crisp links and a frosted Letâs Connect button on the right. Moving from slide 01/03 to 02/03 triggers the siteâs quiet signature. Horizontal rippled bands warp the outgoing room like fluted architectural glass before settling onto Residence Lumiereâs thatched courtyard in Zwevegem, Belgium, and later the dark-paneled lounge of San Franciscoâs D Residence. Minimal controls in the lower-right corner keep that pacing tight.

Stepping past the homepage flips the whole tonal register. On the Selected Projects â24 â â26 index, full-bleed atmosphere gives way to a bright white page and black header chrome, accented only by a solid-black Letâs Connect box and a thin rule beneath the active link. Alphamark staggers the portfolio across two uneven columns so large scenes like Singaporeâs Kage Matcha Bar carry visual weight beside smaller, lower-set previews of Residence Lumiere. A feathered blur along the bottom edge softens incoming rooms and gray one-line captions before they clear into focus. Opening Tiny Apartment pulls back even further: the project title sits alone above an edge-to-edge shelving detail, letting natural light and book spines hold the viewport without sidebar clutter.

That same web design discipline carries into the Studio and Services pages. On the Studio route, a centered three-line statement rests above a stepped five-image strip of stone, travertine, weathered timber, and terracotta vessels, while the paragraph underneath clears gradually from a soft blur as reading continues. Services trades photographic drama for a three-column editorial split separated by a single faint vertical hairline. Left holds Contemporary Interior Design and a black Learn More button; middle lists six plain deliverables from Concept Development to 3D Visualization; right grounds the layout with one vertical room plate. Itâs a calm bit of web design that lets architectural materiality breathe while keeping every link one click away.

NASA Spacecraft Snaps Moody Photo of Earth on Its Way to Mars

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (319 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.
  • Industry observers note that the images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M.
  • The images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.

Industry observers note that the images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M. EST on November 9. This was approximately three hours after the spacecraft made its closest approach to Earth, when it was about 38,500 miles away and had a clear view of the Western Hemisphere.

The images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month. Both spacecraft used a combination of engine burns and Earth’s gravity to gain momentum for their 10-month journey to Mars.

Once they reach orbit around the Red Planet, the spacecraft will study how the solar wind — a stream of charged particles traveling at around a million miles per hour from the Sun — interacts with Mars’ environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

A commercial satellite captured images of the pair from approximately 3,000 miles away, while a member of the mission team photographed the spacecraft passing overhead from his home near Los Angeles (below).

Two spacecraft. Two flybys. One path to Mars.

Photographed from the Los Angeles area, Blue and Gold streaked through the same part of the sky two days apart—Blue in blue, Gold in gold. https://t.co/9SDOMmqqtY.

— Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 23, 2026.

NASA explains that the ESCAPADE mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division and is part of the agency’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission, working with partners including Rocket Lab, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space, and Blue Origin.

Tech Report: Thelma Golden will step down as leader of the Studio Museum in Harlem after 21 years

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired.
  • Industry observers note that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s upcoming six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street.
  • “It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired. Announcing the impending leadership transition on Tuesday (24 November), Kathryn C. Chenault, the chair of the museum’s board, mentioned Golden “is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a upcoming generation she helped foster”.

Industry observers note that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s upcoming six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street. That project had been a focus of much of the past decade of her tenure, including helping to raise a total of $322m as part of a capital campaign supporting construction and growing the museum’s endowment from $5m to $95m. The museum now has significantly more public areas; more galleries for special exhibitions and displays of its public collection; more centrally located studios for its residency programme; a rooftop terrace; and a number of key front- and back-of-house amenities it previously lacked.

“It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening. “The limitations of our two former spaces never stopped this museum from making vital, historic, significant work, it never stopped people from coming and making this a place that was important to them, it never made it so that artists didn’t want to work or engage or show here.

It has been revealed that "However, what it meant to do those things in those spaces often required incredible effort and ingenuity because they weren’t spaces made to be museums, they weren’t spaces made for art. What this space does is it not only increases our physical space, but it allows us to work in ways that we could only dream of in those former spaces.”.

The Studio Museum reopened at 144 West 125th Street in 2025 Photo: © Dror Baldinger FAIA.

According to recent reports, golden’s history at the Studio Museum spans not only her 21 years as its director, but stretches back to her years as an undergraduate student of art history and African American studies at Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts, during which time she had an internship at the museum. After graduation, she stayed on as a curatorial fellow.

According to recent reports, her career then led her to the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she was initially a curatorial assistant, then the director of its off-site programme in Midtown Manhattan, and later an associate curator. During her time there she co-curated the influential 1993 Whitney Biennial (with Elisabeth Sussman) and curated Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art (1994-95), a landmark examination of the construction of Black masculinity through post-war art.

It has been revealed that golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000, when she was hired as the deputy director for exhibitions and programmes, collaborating with the then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. Golden took over the top job in 2005, when Sims stepped down. In addition to her curatorial projects—including a major Chris Ofili show in 2005 and a survey of figuration in African American Art (2002)—Golden became increasingly focused on building the Studio Museum’s future.

When preparations for demolition of its longtime home on 125th Street required the Studio Museum to close in 2018, Golden pursued partnerships with cultural and community organisations in Harlem. Building on a crucial professional development programme created with the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in 2015, she helped launch a multi-year partnership with MoMA and MoMA PS1 in 2019. This led to exhibitions of the Studio Museum’s collection and showcases for the participants in its renowned artist-in-residence programme at those institutions while construction was under way on the new building.

Construction of the Studio Museum’s new home was complicated by both the Covid-19 pandemic, which brought activity to a standstill, and by accusations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against its architect, David Adjaye. (He has denied all the allegations.) The site’s eventual completion and reopening, in November 2025, was seen as a triumph, creating a vastly expanded, purpose-built home for Black art that is equal to the museum’s ambitious programming and stellar permanent collection. The collection was significantly expanded during Golden’s tenure.

Industry observers note that “I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to fresh projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of directors, trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences and beloved Harlem neighbours; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us.”.

In a recent development, as crucial to Golden’s legacy at the Studio Museum as her leadership in the building project is how her work has elevated a newly introduced generation of curators and institutional leaders, and championed artists of the African diaspora who had historically been overlooked. In her work at the Studio Museum and elsewhere, she has provided crucial support for artists including Amy Sherald, Lorna Simpson, Mark Bradford, Simone Leigh and Njideka Akunyili Crosby.

Sources indicate that “She has nurtured the careers of countless artists; she has impacted the arc of art history; she has overseen the construction of a world-class facility in Harlem; and she has transformed the way the public thinks about art of the African diaspora,” Darren Walker, the former president of the Ford Foundation, told The Fresh York Times. (The Ford Foundation endowed the Studio Museum's director position through a $10m grant in 2024.).

Sources indicate that in addition to her role at the Studio Museum, Golden serves on the board of directors of the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation and the Obama Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filmmakers will soon be able to get their hands on the large-format Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 cinema camera for considerably less money than before.

It has been revealed that as NewsShooter reports, a “body-only” version of the GFX Eterna 55 has appeared for preorder at some retailers, including B&H. It costs $9,999, compared to $16,499 for the standard GFX Eterna 55 package.

Saving $6,500 is significant, so what does that extra money actually get video creators?

The standard GFX Eterna 55 includes a custom 5-inch external touchscreen monitor with a mount and hood, a dedicated top handle with customizable controls, and AC power cables. Whether that bundle is worth $6,500 will depend on the individual user, of course.

PetaPixel YouTube host Dmitry Koshutin has used the GFX Eterna 55 extensively and believes the top handle is arguably the camera’s best feature.

“The top handle is probably the best feature of the Eterna,” Koshutin says. “It’s very sturdy, and the controls are very handy. I would still want that, knowing how well it’s built.”.

Recent findings suggest that as of yet, the GFX Eterna 55’s dedicated top handle is not listed as an optional accessory or available for separate purchase. At least for now, the only way for filmmakers to get it is by buying the standard GFX Eterna 55 kit for $16,499.

Industry observers note that koshutin is also a fan of the Eterna’s included external monitor, especially for filming fast-paced action, noting that its proprietary connection works very well. However, he adds that third-party monitors using SDI or HDMI can also be strong alternatives, offering larger or brighter displays.

Recent findings suggest that “Having said that, $10,000 is quite a deal,” Koshutin concludes. “For filmmakers who already own top handle accessories and a monitor, shaving that extra $6,500 off makes a lot of sense without losing much functionality.”.

Industry observers note that the Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 (Body Only) is available for preorder now at $9,999. It is also listed on Fujifilm’s own store, though it is marked “out of stock” and not yet available for preorder there. B&H currently lists the body-only GFX Eterna 55 as “coming soon.”.

Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55Buy new on B&HFujifilm GFX Eterna 55Buy used on KEH.comFujifilm GFX Eterna 55 (Body Only)Buy new on B&HFujifilm GFX Eterna 55 (Body Only)Buy used on KEH.com.

The standard GFX Eterna 55 kit with all the accessories and add-ons remains available for $16,499 and is currently in stock.

Additionally, the dedicated external electronic viewfinder for the GFX Eterna 55 that Fujifilm unveiled in September is expected to ship by the end of December, per B&H. Priced at $1,649.95, it offers GFX Eterna 55 users an alternative way to frame their shots without an external monitor.

#137522. Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (735 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one.
  • The Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts.
  • “The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” says the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one. She became queen of Spain in 1649 after marrying Philip IV, and then when he died in 1665, she assumed the role of regent, governing for over a decade on behalf of their three-year-old son, Charles II. Her authority was challenged, repeatedly. She was also the last woman of the Habsburg dynasty to exercise governing authority within the Spanish court. Even after her regent years were over, Mariana of Austria remained a significant figurehead until her death in 1696.

The Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts. Titled Mariana of Austria, the show reflects the museum’s efforts in recent years to re-examine historic women artists, benefactors and subjects. It includes around 100 objects, from paintings to prints and medals to manuscripts, building up a comprehensive picture of the iconography that Mariana used to curate her own public persona.

“The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” says the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.

Industry observers note that the Prado is poised to host such a presentation since it holds the most comprehensive collection of portraits of Mariana of Austria, representing every stage of her life from her youth as an Austrian archduchess up until her late years as queen mother. A full-length portrait of her by Diego Velázquez, within the Prado collection, was the model for her official image during the early years of her reign.

Frans Luycks, Infanta Mariana of Austria (around 1646)Museo Nacional del Prado.

Mariana of Austria was in good company among other European royals who understood that authority needed a visual translation, to be communicated both domestically and across Europe. Some of the iconographic devices used by her court painters had precedents elsewhere, including among other queens. Such strategies include the use of the seated portrait, which was traditionally associated with ruling princes, and portraits in which she held a document as a reference to her governing ability.

Recent findings suggest that preparation of the exhibition has led to both a different understanding of such iconography, and a deeper knowledge of the works themselves, thanks to restorations and a reassessment of dates, identifications and attributions of several works. The exhibition also reunites rarely seen and never before exhibited works, such as a double portrait of Mariana of Austria and Charles II, on loan from the Bečov nad Teplou Castle in the Czech Republic, and a bust attributed to Nicolás de Bussy, which was recently identified as a portrait of the queen.

It has been revealed that another section of the exhibition is devoted to portraits of queens, regents and other female governors who held power within the Spanish monarchy over the course of roughly two centuries. “Seeing these works together reveals how attributes such as the book and the column were passed down and acquired upcoming meanings from one generation to the next,” Garcia Pérez indicates, “gradually shaping a shared visual language in which piety, dynastic legitimacy and the exercise of power were closely intertwined.”.

Mariana of Austria culminates a year of focusing on three queens at the Prado—Elisabeth Farnese, Christina of Sweden and now Mariana of Austria—exploring not only their tastes but also how they used the arts as a means of asserting their authority. This focus is part of the Prado’s commitment, over the past decade, to highlight the multifaceted roles of women in art history. These initiatives have evolved into the long-term programme called The Female Perspective, which will investigate the influence of Europe’s ruling women on the arts in collaboration with the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

Recent findings suggest that the next exhibition in the works will focus on female patrons of the 19th century, highlighting figures such as Spain’s Isabella II. “Ultimately, the ambition of The Female Perspective is not simply to add women’s names to an established narrative,” Garcia Pérez claims. “But to enrich and, where necessary, rethink that narrative.”.

• Mariana of Austria, Museo Nacional del Prado, Madrid, until 28 March 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, has been out in the wild for a month now, and more apps are being updated to natively support the dual-screened device all the time. Adobe Lightroom just got a major iPhone Duo compatibility patch this week, and it is a strong example of how good the Duo can be.

As Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom Product Designer, Johannes Eckert, explains on Threads, the Adobe team has worked hard to fully optimize Lightroom for Duo.

The iPhone Duo version of Lightroom works as normal on the device’s front screen, but when opened up, it is an entirely transformed experience, showing photos much larger than on other iPhone models and moving editing tools to the side. There’s also a “laptop pose,” as Eckert notes, that puts editing tools on the bottom while the photo stays above the fold.

Recent findings suggest that in PetaPixel‘s testing, the updated app worked as promised and delivered a genuinely pleasant mobile photo editing experience. It’s nice to see my photos on the Duo’s large internal screen and to be able to access sliders, presets, masking tools, and more without obscuring my photo at all or needing to shrink it way down. You can still actually see your photo while utilizing Lightroom’s suite of editing tools, which is a big improvement over a standard iPhone photo editing experience.

It has been revealed that that said, there is still some room for improvement, and it seems like Adobe is already working on making tweaks. For example, when doing a Curves edit, the curves themselves appear on as an overlay on the photo, which is fine, except that it leaves much of the Duo’s inner screen totally empty.

“I think it’s better to have the curves to [the] right to get rid of the empty space,” Threads user itsrongarcia commented on Eckert’s original post.

“We agree. This will be in the next upgrade!” Eckert replied.

Other people are looking forward to Adobe bringing some of its more powerful editing tools over from iPad, arguing that Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip is more than capable of running things like automatic dust removal and AI-powered noise reduction. There’s no word yet on whether Adobe is considering these things at this time.

Recent findings suggest that adobe will no doubt refine the iPhone Duo version of Lightroom further as more real-world owners get to test it out and offer their feedback, but so far, so good. Ultimately, the iPhone Duo’s lasting appeal will depend heavily on how apps utilize its distinct form factor. Lightroom is definitely taking full advantage of it, and Lightroom mobile has never been as enjoyable to use.

  • Industry observers note that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.

Industry observers note that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004. The images document a period when free parties were spreading across Europe, offering an alternative to mainstream society through music, community, and a shared rejection of conventional lifestyles.

Sources indicate that rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture. Their photographs provide a firsthand account of a counterculture built around emotion, affection, and togetherness, at a time when music and personal connections — rather than social media and mass communication — brought people together.

It has been revealed that the book spans 196 black-and-white pages and brings together previously unseen photographs that capture the atmosphere and values of the era. Its accompanying text is written by Tobia D’Onofrio, author of Rave Upcoming World, who explores the history and significance of the European free-party movement.

“Rave was born as a disappearing ritual in which the art of invisibility was practiced, and parties were temporarily autonomous and free zones that appeared and disappeared into thin air within a few hours,” states D’Onofrio.

It has been revealed that “1997–2004 can therefore be considered the golden age of the so-called illegal free parties and of rave culture. It was the moment of the phenomenon’s expansion across Europe… the rave scene had been criminalized to the point that in 1994 the Criminal Justice Act in England outlawed free parties. At that point, the energies shifted to the rest of Europe, and Italy immediately became the scene of legendary parties.”.

The book examines how rave culture developed into more than a musical movement. It represented a rejection of conventional working and social structures, embracing communal living, constant movement, and a different relationship with time and space. Free parties became meeting places for people united by anarchic sensibilities and a desire to escape everyday routines.

Clementi and Morandi both attended the same high school in Milan before pursuing separate careers. Despite taking different paths, both remained dedicated to photography, eventually bringing their shared rave-scene experiences together in Never Alone.

The book is available online and through specialist bookstores.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A student photographer who lost his right eye after he was allegedly struck by a projectile fired by a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent while covering a “No Kings” protest is suing the federal government.

Warning: The following photos contain content that some may find upsetting.

Industry observers note that tucker Collins, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Southern California (USC), was left partially blind after photographing demonstrators in downtown Los Angeles on the afternoon of March 28. Collins was allegedly photographing a confrontation between protesters and federal agents when he was allegedly hit by a less-lethal projectile.

Footage demonstrates Collins taking pictures of demonstrators outside a federal facility before suddenly falling to his knees as a crowd-control projectile reportedly struck him in the right eye, fracturing bones in his eye socket. Collins was taken to a hospital, where he underwent two and a half hours of surgery in an attempt to save the eye. The injury was too severe, and the eye was surgically removed.

It has been revealed that collins sued the federal government on Monday, alleging that law enforcement officers used excessive force and violated his civil rights. According to a report by The Fresh York Times, his attorneys allege that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers “assaulted” and “used unjustified force against him” as he photographed the protest.

The lawsuit seeks various damages from the federal government, “including past and future medical expenses, prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, educational expenses, and loss of earning capacity.”.

According to recent reports, collins’s attorney, V. James DeSimone, and his family are also demanding criminal charges against the officer responsible for shooting him. They argue that the officer’s actions violated California law governing the use of projectile launchers by law enforcement.

The lawsuit also details how Collins’s injuries have limited his ability to pursue activities he once enjoyed, including photography. Collins claims he is no longer able to safely photograph public events similar to the protest where he was injured. DeSimone also condemned the lack of criminal accountability in the wake of the shooting.

Sources indicate that “It is deeply disturbing that the maiming of Tucker Collins, resulting in the loss of his eye, was widely reported and captured on video and, yet, there is no law enforcement response, to date, on the Federal, State or Local level to prosecute the offending officer for his crime,” DeSimone says in a statement. “Once again, it is left to civil rights attorneys to attempt to achieve some semblance of justice for the permanent and irreversible harm caused to this courageous young man.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DixonBaxi sets the EA SPORTS FC 27 brand identity free, turning one triangle into dozens of forms built to move, remix and belong to fans.

The triangle was already the mark. FC spent three years building something millions love, and DixonBaxi kept the shape at the centre of it rather than redrawing it. The studio set it loose instead. One triangle now arrives as a wireframe outline, a dotted halftone field, a pixelated edge, a solid green slab or a beam of light, and the identity holds together because the shape never changes, only the way it behaves. The line on the posters states it plainly: FC is not played, it is lived.

According to recent reports, type does the loud work. The grid sheet sets EVERYONE'S PLAYING in stacked condensed caps, with the FC27 lockup held to two columns and the tagline stretched across five, and the annotations name the voice: Cruyff Sans Condensed Medium for the calls to action, Cruyff Sans Regular for the small print. THE WORLD'S GAME runs the same way on the billboards, the heavy word GAME dropped below a tracked-out THE WORLD'S in the same condensed face.

The grid behind it all is the triangle itself. Lines flow across the posters the way crowds move, and the lockups sit inside the same diagonal geometry, so a headline, a phone screen and a stadium banner all read as one system. The palette stays close to the pitch: electric green leads, with hot pink, purple and blue in support, and black fields that let the colour shout.

Sources indicate that the system proves itself on real objects. A green controller carries the triangle pattern across its shell, with the FC27 lockup set into the touchpad in pale gold. The Grounds, the open world where players meet, compete and chat beyond the pitch, gets its own mark: FC set inside a heavy triangle, with SCREEN, STADIUM and STREET as its three corners, and ten small variants beneath it in pink, purple, green and white.

The launch trailer pulled 5+ million views on day one, and the same triangles now run from campaign posters to the game itself, built for a community the studio counts at one billion fans. Make it your Club, your City, your Crew, your Home, your Block: the identity hands the shape to the fans and lets them finish it.

Recent findings suggest that BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

It has been revealed that layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tate Liverpool will reopen next autumn following an extensive four-year redevelopment costing around £30m. The relaunch programme includes a major show dedicated to Surrealism along with the first major retrospective for the Liverpool-based artist Chila Kumari Singh Burman. The key regional UK gallery, located on the city’s Royal Albert Dock, closed in October 2023 and was initially due to reopen in 2025.

Chila Kumari Singh Burman in front of her Winter Commission covering the façade of Tate Britain in London in 2020.

Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others. “The show will reveal the crucial role of Surrealism in the history of theatre and dance, from experiments with masquerade, character and role play to major commissions for stage sets and costumes,” notes a Tate statement. Works featured include Claude Cahun's photograph of Sheila Legge’s 1936 performance Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal, when the artist wore a Dalí-inspired costume in London's Trafalgar Square.

Claude Cahun, Sheila Legge as Surrealist ‘Phantom’, Trafalgar Square (1936).

© Claude Cahun; Image courtesy Jersey Heritage Collections.

Industry observers note that for the overhaul, Tate Liverpool received £18.6m from the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, which is awarded by the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. It also received philanthropic donations from the Garfield Weston Foundation (£3m), the Wolfson Foundation (£1.25m) and the Ross Warburton Charitable Trust, alongside other trusts and individuals.

The UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also awarded £10m to the gallery, which it secured through a combined £20m bid with National Museums Liverpool. “We have raised more [than £30m] because there are other costs associated with reinstalling and reopening the museum,” a Tate spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper.

According to a Tate statement, the designs for the fresh gallery, drawn up by 6a architects, “open up spaces to display the incredible variety of Tate’s collection and host world-class exhibitions. These galleries will sit alongside new public spaces for play, relaxation and learning with views across the Mersey, helping to connect the gallery with the city and the communities that surround it.” The New York and Berlin-based artist Asad Raza will create the first major commission for the gallery’s Art Hall.

Recent findings suggest that tate Liverpool, which opened in 1988, was designed by James Stirling who converted the northwest corner of a seven-story warehouse standing on the Royal Albert Dock into the five-storey gallery. It received 405,000 visitors in 2022, its last full year, and 660,000 in 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic.

Helen Legg stepped down as Tate Liverpool director earlier this year, with Jemima Pyne taking over in the interim; a new director will be recruited after the new director of Tate, Jessica Morgan, is in post next year, the spokesperson confirmed. Tate comprises four galleries: Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a spectacular video of a moonset yesterday (Tuesday) from onboard the International Space Station.

The mesmerizing footage highlights Earth’s natural satellite melting into the atmosphere as it disappears behind Earth.

“This is a real-time video of a moonset today from the space station cupola on a [Nikon] Z9 and 400mm lens,” Menon writes on his Instagram page.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Menon also shared a series of photos, which he specifically states contain “no edits or alterations.” Menon, a colonel in the United States Space Force, flew to the ISS in July 2026 as part of Expedition 75, for which he is a flight engineer.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Not too long after he joined the floating space station, Menon snapped a mind-boggling photo of a super typhoon brooding above the Pacific Ocean — on his iPhone.

Just like the moonset photos, Menon took the typhoon photo from the space station’s cupola, a dome-shaped panoramic observatory module featuring six circumferential windows and a central nadir viewing window.

It has been revealed that the cupola is where so much of the fantastic photography is made on the ISS. Menon recently shared a behind-the-scenes video showing how astronauts set up shots inside the seven-sided window.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

According to recent reports, “Welcome to the cupola,” claims Menon. “This is a camera. That’s planet Earth. Here are our seven windows that we can look down at Earth with, and I’m going to take this camera and set it up for a night shot.”.

During the video, day is slowly turning to night. “Because we’re going to take a long exposure, we need to keep it stable, so we’ll set the camera up in the window, tighten it up so it’s stable, and we can put in our settings,” Menon explains.

“But a lot of light is going to leak in from the sides because there’s a lot of LEDs around; there are power strips and things that can get in, so we put this shroud over the camera. That way, the lens is facing out at planet Earth, and it is hidden from the light.”.

Last week, PetaPixel highlighted German astronaut Rabea Rogge loading 35mm film into her SLR camera while in zero-gravity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.
  • In a recent development, jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to a report by The Newly introduced York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.

In a recent development, jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations. An estimated 4,500 Jehovah’s Witnesses were sent to concentration camps.

Recent findings suggest that according to a report by The Newly introduced York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Two of the couple’s sons were executed after refusing military service because of their religious beliefs. The three youngest children were taken from their family and placed in a Nazi training school, where they were prohibited from contacting their relatives. Both parents and their remaining children were sentenced to prison terms.

One of their daughters Annemarie Kusserow was arrested by the Gestapo in October 1944 and remained a prisoner until May 25, 1945, after the war in Europe had ended. Over the following decades, Annemarie gathered and preserved a collection of more than 1,000 photographs, documents, drawings, letters, and reports documenting her family’s experiences.

In her 2005 will, Annemarie bequeathed the entire photo archive to the German headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. However, her brother Hans Werner Kusserow, to whom she had loaned the collection for research purposes, sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2009. The archive has remained in the German museum’s possession ever since.

According to the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website, the sale of the photo collection to a military museum was “especially troubling” given that two of Annemarie’s brothers had lost their lives because of their pacifist beliefs. The organization states the sale of the archive “resulted in years of legal battles.”.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses filed a lawsuit to recover the archive from the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, which is operated by the German armed forces. On November 19, the museum and the religious organization reached an “amicable agreement” under which the collection will be handed over to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Both parties have agreed to keep the terms of the settlement confidential.

According to The New York Times, Sebastian Stock, a spokesman for the religious organization in Germany, says that once the transfer is complete, the “Jehovah’s Witnesses will develop and present a concept for making the archive accessible for further academic research.”.

In addition to digitizing the archive and making it available to scholars, the Jehovah’s Witnesses initiative to display some of the documents in a new exhibition examining the history of the religious group in Central Europe.

Recent findings suggest that zanele Muholi, Zanele Muholi, Tembisa, Johannesburg, 2014, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

According to recent reports, muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Industry observers note that zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

Zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

The people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have said. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

Zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

In a recent development, zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Sources indicate that they discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?

This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.

It has been revealed that bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with upcoming guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. You can also explore the related exhibition in La Petite Galerie, called Everyday Clothing, which allows young visitors and families to explore the creative process through works from the MEP’s collections.

On the paired exhibition posters, a black monochrome marble-sculpture layout sits beside a coral-red graphic sheet where the oversized white mark anchors staggered FIND LOVE HERE lettering. According to recent reports, GTA 6 is having a wider impact than just being one of the highest-rated games ever, with a 99 on Metacritic; it’s making other developers rethink what they’re doing. This week, many devs came out and praised GTA 6’s technical achievements, from CD Projekt Red to Naughty Dog, but behind the scenes, those same creators are setting new benchmarks to complete.

The impact of GTA 6 is simple: it’s as impressive as all great art is, because it expands what's possible through a captivating vision and flawless execution. And it’s making developers think and rethink.

CD Projekt Red is no slouch when it comes to technically advanced games and graphics, but even they are having that moment. The studio behind The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 has admitted that GTA 6 inspires its developers, with joint CEO Michał Nowakowski saying he expects The Witcher 4 to make a similarly huge leap over its predecessor.

As reported on Polygon, speaking during the tech giant's latest investor call, Nowakowski was asked whether the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 would be comparable to the one between GTA 5 and GTA 6. His answer was pretty emphatic.

"Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes," he said. "I mean, it's been 11 years.".

The studio is working to make The Witcher 4 "significantly better-looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game", adding that players should expect a much bigger jump between the two games.

Sources indicate that that's quite a promise, although there's a good reason to be ambitious. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is now 11 years old, and while its world still looks fantastic (especially after its recent remaster), the technology and expectations for open-world games have moved on considerably.

In a recent development, GTA 6 is an obvious comparison, but I'm more interested in what CD Projekt Red does differently. Rockstar has its own way of building a world, and The Witcher's appeal has always been its atmosphere, character design, and strong writing. I don't need Ciri's world to look like Vice City, but I do want the same depth and sense of a living world Rockstar has created. Following this year’s Unreal Engine 5.6 tech demo, I’m sure The Witcher 4 will impress, possibly setting a new standard.

It has been revealed that CD Projekt Red is clearly putting a lot of its development resources into The Witcher 4. Its latest figures show 513 developers working on the game, compared with 199 on Cyberpunk 2. The latter is still in the earlier stages of development, so expect that team to grow. The Witcher 4 is right now targeting a 2028 release, while Cyberpunk 2 is further away, and by that time we’ll be in the realms of PlayStation 6 and Unreal Engine 6.

According to recent reports, there's also a question of how much money studios need to spend to reach these fresh visual standards. Nowakowski was keen to stress that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt Red's development philosophy, describing its projects as ambition-driven rather than simply budget-driven.

Perhaps that's where the GTA 6 hype is sidelined: few developers have Rockstar’s billion-dollar budgets, and no indie ever will, but CD Projekt Red has UE6 and faith in its artists, technicians, and writers. You still need artists with a clear idea of what they want to create, and developers who know how to bring that vision to life.

These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.

The move is simple and hard to argue with. Instead of inventing a new symbol, JKR took the one object every KFC customer already knows and made it the system. The bucket is now a frame: it holds food photography, illustration and campaign lines, and it scales from a cup to a building. The logo itself turns three dimensional, the Colonel gets a warmer expression and a collar under his bow tie, and the red, white and black palette stays exactly where it was. Nothing about the brand gets thrown out. Everything gets pointed at the bucket.

Two custom typefaces carry the voice. Kentucky Fried Serif and Kentucky Fried Sans were drawn with StudioDRAMA, and the serif does the heavy lifting: it spells KFC at poster scale on the bucket, the bag and the building, with thick strokes and tight spacing that read from across a street. The stripes, once a background pattern, are reworked into a type-based asset that carries its own messages, and the boxes repeat lines like BIG KFC FLAVOR DIALED UP TO 11 and NOTHING HITS LIKE KFC ORIGINAL CHICKEN in stacked red caps. Tobias Hall drew the Finger Lickin' Good lettering, which now works as a mark in its own right, set in script against the block serif.

The system holds together because the same decisions repeat at every size. The kraft bag carries the serif wordmark at full height. The restaurant facade draws the bucket outline across the whole frontage in white line on red, with the Colonel sitting above the door. Inside, curved screens run giant red letterforms behind the counter, and the KWENCH drinks range gets its own vertical sign. A global roster of illustrators adds the colour: Bernardo Henning's loose, bright drawing fills the back of a black T-shirt, and a silver bucket pendant turns the packaging into jewellery. The photography follows the same rule, shot from inside the bucket looking up, so the food and the people sit inside the frame the brand built.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that brightin Star first unveiled its latest APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH.
  • The Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH.
  • Sources indicate that although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that brightin Star first unveiled its latest APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras at CP+ in February and then introduced it on Kickstarter in August. As of today, it’s available to everyone, and it’s still as handsome as ever.

The Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. is a full-frame, manual-focus lens with a native Leica M-Mount design. However, as evidenced by the fact that Brightin Star offers it in kits with E, Z, RF, X, L, and even GFX adapters, it’s easy to adapt to other camera systems. Although Brightin Star does not state the lens’s exact image circle when used with its GFX adapter, the manufacturer says it covers the 44 x 33-millimeter sensor inside GFX system medium-format mirrorless cameras.

Sources indicate that although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted. Brightin Star notes that 100 degrees of focus throw covers infinity to 0.7 meters, while an additional 207 degrees covers the relatively narrow distance from 0.3 to 0.7 meters. That 307 degrees of total focus rotation is quite a lot, and Brightin Star describes it as “cinema style.”.

Sources indicate that the 35mm f/1.7 prime is a compact, relatively lightweight lens. It measures just 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs around 260 grams (9.2 ounces). It accepts 39mm front filters. Part of Brightin Star’s new “Apex” series of lenses, the 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. promises precision build quality and high-end optical performance.

Sources indicate that “We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star claims. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.”.

According to recent reports, on the topic of image quality, the lens features 11 elements arranged across seven groups. There are some notable elements inside, including three double-sided aspherical lenses, three high-refractive pieces of glass, and an ED element. There are also two floating lens groups that move independently during focusing, which the manufacturer says better controls distance-related aberrations and reduces spherical aberrations at close range. The lens also promises minimized focus breathing.

In a recent development, as evidenced by the “APO” in its name, Brightin Star says this is an “apochromatic” lens. While there’s no precise, industry-standard definition for what level of performance that requires, Brightin Star promises minimal chromatic aberration. An apochromatic lens focuses red, blue, and green wavelengths of light at the exact same point on the image plane. The closer a lens gets to achieving this ideal, the fewer chromatic aberrations it exhibits, all else being equal.

It has been revealed that the Brightin Star MF 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. lens is available now for $1,099 for Leica M. An adapter adds $30, pushing the price to $1,129.

Latest Update: Christie’s acquires British auction house Dreweatts

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christie's confirmed today it has acquired the British auction house Dreweatts, a move that confirms the enduring appeal of antiques and older collectibles, particularly as profits in other parts of the auction sector remain squeezed.
  • In a recent development, both businesses will run as before, Christie’s confirms, with no staffing changes expected as a result of the deal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christie's confirmed today it has acquired the British auction house Dreweatts, a move that confirms the enduring appeal of antiques and older collectibles, particularly as profits in other parts of the auction sector remain squeezed.

In a recent development, both businesses will run as before, Christie’s confirms, with no staffing changes expected as a result of the deal. Dreweatts will retain its name and continue to be run “independently” by its chief executive, Henry House, and chairman Will Richards, according to a Christie's statement. Dreweatts will continue to operate from its salesroom at Donnington Priory in Newbury, Berkshire, with no sales expected to move to London.

Dreweatts, founded in 1759, is best known for country house and estate sales, and its specialist departments covering furniture, Old Masters, ceramics, jewellery, silver, clocks and wine. It holds around 70 sales a year. In 2025, it posted a record total auction turnover of £37.56m (£47.3m with fees)—a 26% increase from its 2024 results. Both Christie’s and Dreweatts are privately owned and do not disclose their profits.

A display ahead of the sale of Patrick and Amabel Lindsay’s collection at Dreweatts.

In a recent development, the acquisition in some ways sees Christie’s backtrack its 2017 decision to close its South Kensington venue, known as Christie's South Kensington or CSK, which specialised in antiques and other traditional collecting categories. This decision was taken as the market for postwar and contemporary art was at its peak, and as the trade chased global expansion and billionaire tastes at the expense of localism and connoisseurship.

Today, auctions of Modern and postwar trophy lots might generate more glamour and headlines than high-volume and lower-value antiques sales, but the overheads for winning these prize consignments devours profit margins. Indeed, many leading industry figures criticised Christie’s decision to close CSK as a shortsighted one that haemorrhaged valuable strongholds of specialist knowledge and alienated potential new buyers.

Christie's president Bonnie Brennan says in a statement that Dreweatts possesses “particular strength in a part of the market that is highly complementary to our own. Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service.”.

This marks the second major acquisition of a smaller auction house by Christie’s in recent years, following the 2024 buyout of the classic car vendors Gooding & Firm.

Sources indicate that christie’s acquires Dreweatts from the advisory firm Gurr Johns, which bought the regional auction house in 2017 for £1.25m, as The Art Newspaper reported at the time. “I believe that Christie’s is the only business with the capacity, experience and shared culture to fulfil the further potential of Dreweatts,”, Gurr Johns chief told the Financial Times.

AI-Generated Characters Are Stealing Content Creators’ Viral Videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.
  • From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.
  • Industry observers note that the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.

From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.

Industry observers note that the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools. People can take an existing video and replace the original performer with an artificial character, often designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualized.

The Instagram page More Perfect Union points to Higgsfield AI and its upcoming Genjutsu tool that allows consumers to upload any video file and remix it with the user’s own character, locations, or product. However, other elements of the video remain untouched.

Just a few weeks ago, Nvidia invested in Higgsfield AI in a Series B funding round that raised $400 million. It gave Higgsfield a valuation of $5.4 billion.

A post shared by More Perfect Union (@perfectunion).

Sophie Lloyd, a U.K.-based guitarist who tours with U.S. rapper Machine Gun Kelly, tells the BBC she has spent years building an online following, only to see AI accounts reproduce content created by musicians and other performers.

“A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we’ve created,” Lloyd says.

In a recent development, dr. Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, tells the British broadcaster that the practice is often less about experimentation with AI and more about exploiting content that has already demonstrated its popularity.

“What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that’s already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools,” she indicates.

While some accounts may use the technology for entertainment, Kendall says others are deliberately copying successful videos in the hope of attracting an audience and generating revenue.

According to recent reports, she sees the trend as part of a wider online “hustle culture,” in which accounts look to turn attention and engagement into money. That can mean directing followers toward subscription-based fan pages featuring adult content, promoting risky cryptocurrency products such as meme coins, or simply taking advantage of monetization features offered by social media platforms.

For the original creators, identifying and stopping the accounts responsible can be extremely difficult.

Alwyn Cruz, who has built a following on social media by exposing AI-generated musicians, describes trying to shut down these accounts as a game of whack-a-mole.

It has been revealed that “You don’t even know who’s making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they’re just going to create another,” he states.

Cruz claims the problem extends well beyond musicians, with performers from a variety of disciplines finding their work replicated.

“It’s not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I’ve seen this all over the internet.”.

The accessibility of AI reskinning tools like Higgsfield means the practice could become increasingly difficult to contain. Creators can spend years developing an online presence and refining a style that audiences recognize, only to find that the same performances can be reproduced with a different face and a few clicks.

And while the AI-generated versions may be attracting attention, the people behind the original performances are often left watching someone else benefit from their work.

Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.

Recent findings suggest that according to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years. FoodShare is Wisconsin’s food assistance program for individuals and families with limited incomes.

According to a report by Fox 11 News, an investigation was launched after Dodge County Economic Support uncovered apparent inconsistencies between Miller’s tax records, employment records, court documents, and applications for public assistance.

Authorities allege that the photographer provided inaccurate information about her income and residency when applying for benefits, including failing to disclose earnings from her business Fawn Focus Photography.

Between 2019 and 2025, Miller allegedly received more than $30,000 in FoodShare benefits that she was not entitled to claim. She also received more than $22,000 in childcare assistance benefits, although investigators were still determining how much of that funding was improperly obtained.

According to online court records, Miller faces six counts of failing to disclose an event affecting her eligibility for benefits and six counts of failing to report the receipt of income or assets. The photographer made her initial court appearance this month and was issued a $5,000 signature bond.

“Public assistance programs exist to help individuals and families during times of genuine need and are funded by hardworking taxpayers,” Dodge County Sheriff Dale J. Schmidt tells Fox 11 News in a statement. “When someone is alleged to have concealed income or provided false information in order to obtain benefits, it undermines public trust and diverts limited resources away from those who legitimately qualify for assistance.”.

Sources indicate that previously, PetaPixel reported on a photographer who was sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a family out of $4.6 million and using $200,000 of the money to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets. 46-year-old photographer Chanise Coyne was given jail time after pleading guilty to wire fraud over a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme involving fictional child modeling events.

This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists.
  • Industry observers note that A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't.
  • It has been revealed that this optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

Industry observers note that A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of big debate.

It has been revealed that this optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

The problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

According to recent reports, they note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

It has been revealed that amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

But one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.

With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that spain’s snap elections, due to take place on 29 November, have left several long-awaited new measures and legislation for art and culture hanging in the balance. These include regulations on AI, intellectual property and artist welfare. With a coalition between the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party looking increasingly likely, here is what the vote could mean for the country’s art and culture sector.

Recent findings suggest that the future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election. PP has argued in favour of maintaining it, albeit merged with other portfolios, but Vox will only support the ministry’s existence if cultural powers at the moment held by Spain’s autonomous communities are transferred to the central government.

In a recent development, the prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections. At a party meeting on 22 November, Vox’s secretary general, Ignacio Garriga, stated that they will support cultural professionals who “create quality national products” and “highlight the value of the country's culture”.

Even if the ministry of culture continues, the sector expects budget cuts under a PP-Vox coalition. The PP has pledged to rapidly pass a new patronage law with tax and legal incentives to encourage private businesses and individuals to fund cultural projects, arguing that healthcare and defence spending will leave culture underfunded by the state. The PP's proposals for culture also include auditing working conditions, exhibition standards and security protocols across national museums.

Industry observers note that the Status of the Artist bill, a welfare package designed to improve working conditions of those in the cultural sector, will enter into force in 2027 regardless of the election results, after being approved by the Council of Ministers in July. However, the inclusion of visual artists—who, unlike other types of artists, were entirely left out of the bill and continue to face prohibitive self-employment quotas—remains up in the air.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, the Union of Contemporary Artists of Spain rolled out a campaign to push for their inclusion with the support of the ministry of culture, but the decision stalled in the ministries of social security and finance. Gloria Reguero, the president of the union, says that they have been waiting since 2018 for painters, sculptors and photographers to be recognised as artists. “Just when it seemed we were going to start negotiating our terms, the elections came along, and with them, another setback,” she tells The Art Newspaper.

Meanwhile, a separate draft bill regulating the use of generative AI in the arts is not getting off the ground at all. The legislation was put out for public consultation in late September and it marked the government’s third attempt to regulate AI in the arts following two failed royal decrees. The draft bill sought to prohibit the use of generative AI to exploit an artist’s image, voice or work without their express consent and specific remuneration and, like the Status of the Artist, it left out the visual arts.

Both PP and Vox have strongly opposed prepares by Ernest Urtasun, the current Spanish culture minister, to review state museum collections—specifically the Museum of the Americas and the National Museum of Anthropology—to “move past a colonial framework”. When the initiative was first announced in early 2024, the PP dismissed the push for decolonisation, in a statement, as “a false debate, imposed and manufactured to create division among Spaniards”.

In November 2025, the ministry formally presented a €13.6m project to overhaul the permanent exhibitions and narratives of both institutions through an “anti-racist and gender perspective”.

In a recent development, ahead of the elections, the project has reached different stages: while the National Museum of Anthropology has already moved through its public tendering process for the remodelling of its permanent exhibition, the Museum of the Americas remains at an earlier stage, with major works still pending. If a newly introduced government takes office, the initiative’s long-term completion, scheduled for 2028, faces significant uncertainty—with a risk that yet-to-be-contracted tenders may be halted or that curatorial direction may be revised. A spokesperson for the Museum of the Americas declined to respond to The Art Newspaper's request for comment, “especially now that we’re on the eve of the elections and everything is so uncertain”, they say.

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

According to recent reports, the star of the show for the Rochester, Newly introduced York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” claims Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

Sources indicate that “We continue to execute our long-term plan and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an key indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

As Continenza notes, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

Industry observers note that while Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak says award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

“The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too promptly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film company routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

In a recent development, paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few big names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

It has been revealed that then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some fresh, albeit familiar, ones. The organization reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

Between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.
